analysis.one_liner: Bans drug makers from "product hopping" to delay cheaper generic competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop brand-name drug makers from delaying cheaper generics drew 16 Senate cosponsors and cleared the Judiciary Committee in July 2021, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it an unfair method of competition for a brand-name drug maker to pull its drug off the market, or quietly disadvantage it, in order to push patients onto a tweaked version with a later-expiring patent — a tactic called "product hopping" that blocks cheaper generics. The Federal Trade Commission could enforce the ban and claw back profits. It would also cap, with exceptions, how many patents a brand-name biologic maker can wield in a lawsuit against a biosimilar competitor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs facing an imminent generic or biosimilar competitor would benefit if the bill passed, because the switch-to-a-tweaked-version tactic that keeps prices high would carry legal risk. Insurers, employers, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid would also pay less, and generic and biosimilar manufacturers would find it easier to enter the market.

how_it_helps.text: It makes 'product hopping' — withdrawing a drug or stacking the deck against it to move patients onto a follow-on version with a later-expiring patent — an unfair method of competition that the FTC can prosecute, with a presumption of violation when a maker pulls its drug after learning a generic application has been filed.

It gives the FTC real teeth: the agency could sue in federal court, win injunctions, and order drug makers to disgorge the extra profits they earned from the delay, plus restitution, for up to five years after the enrichment.

It caps, at 20 patents (no more than 10 filed late in the drug's life), how many patents a brand-name biologic maker can assert in an infringement suit against a biosimilar applicant, limiting the 'patent thicket' strategy used to stall competitors for years.

It keeps legitimate improvements on the table: changes the FDA demands, safety-driven reformulations, and truthful marketing are explicitly excluded from the ban, and makers can rebut the presumption by showing they would have acted anyway.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose a profitable way to extend monopolies past patent expiry — including possible court-ordered disgorgement of profits already earned from delayed competition. Enforcement costs would fall on the FTC and the courts, and some patent litigation over biosimilars would shift in the biosimilar makers' favor.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is litigation-heavy and slow: manufacturers can rebut the presumption by arguing they would have made the change anyway, or for safety or pro-competitive reasons, and the FTC must then prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the conduct's anticompetitive harms outweigh its benefits — meaning cases could drag on for years while patients keep paying.

The patent cap has escape hatches: a court can raise the 20-patent limit for 'good cause' or 'the interest of justice', and method-of-use patents are entirely exempt, so a determined brand-name maker may still assemble enough patents to stall a biosimilar.

Drug makers' standard objection to this kind of bill is that weaker and shorter-lived exclusivity reduces the revenue that funds research into new medicines; the bill tries to answer this by protecting genuinely safety-driven changes, but the line between a real improvement and a monopoly-extending one would be fought case by case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: product hopping and patent thickets are documented ways brand-name makers keep prices high after patents lapse, and the bill attacks both with an FTC enforcement tool that includes clawbacks. The costs are modest and fall almost entirely on a single profitable industry, though the bill is not airtight — rebuttable presumptions, carve-outs, and judicial exceptions could blunt it, and it leaves other delay strategies untouched. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection measure whose main cost is to the companies it regulates. Its fatal weakness was not design but the fact that it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it in July 2021, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2023, so it died.

narrative.text: Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, together with Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), and it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee.
Sixteen senators cosponsored it — 10 of 48 Senate Democrats, 5 of 50 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents — an unusual bipartisan lineup for a drug-pricing bill.
On July 29, 2021, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, moving it one step toward the floor.
No further action followed: the bill never received a floor vote, never passed a chamber, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they keep the ability to extend monopoly pricing through product switches and patent thickets, while patients continue to bear the higher prices that the bill would have risked for them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and their patents

for.name: John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Judiciary Committee, which ordered it reported favorably.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined Cornyn in introducing the bill, supplying the Democratic half of a bipartisan sponsor team.

for.name: 16 senators: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats, 5 of 50 Senate Republicans, 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 29, 2021.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor despite its committee approval, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restrictions on patent strategies and product switching that would erode brand-name drug exclusivity.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split across parties — 10 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — and the committee approved it unanimously reported, but because the bill never reached a floor vote the Senate's actual partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: These companies profit by extending monopoly pricing past patent expiry — switching patients to reformulated versions or burying biosimilar rivals in patent suits. The bill would have made the first tactic legally actionable with profit clawbacks and capped the second, directly cutting into a major revenue strategy.

Fewer patents to litigate and less risk of a brand-name maker yanking the reference drug off the shelf would lower the cost and risk of launching competing products — the same outcome that lowers prices for patients.

industries.industry: Health insurers, employers, and government health programs
industries.note: Payers like Medicare, Medicaid, and employer plans absorb much of the cost of extended brand-name monopolies, so faster generic and biosimilar entry would reduce their drug spending.
